questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose Edinburgh because I had family who previously attended the University, some of whom were still living in the city. They had very positive things to say about the academic environment and city alike.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: 10 socially, but maybe a 6 academically. That's why I chose 8.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The University website is very accessible and covers pretty much every aspect of moving to the city.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: 5, because I was satisfied with whatever information was available on the website. I didn't need any assistance upon arrival, but I had the impression that it was available through student services if need be.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I was VERY lucky to find private housing. I contacted someone through a facebook-post about a room in an area I was interested in, but that particular room had 45 applicants. Relatedly, the housing market in Edinburgh is probably the biggest downside of choosing to study abroad at the University of Edinburgh. It is important to know that the University can be quite helpful if you're an undergrad (Danish bachelor's student), but that they do not provide any assistance if you're a postgrad visiting from Europe. 

I would recommend keeping an eye on facebook groups and websites like spareroom as soon as your mobility is confirmed. Also, most private housing is administered by agencies that can have quite strict rules for deposits, UK-based guarantors etc. However, if you do manage to find a room, it can be an incredibly cool experience!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Edinburgh is small enough to walk from pretty much any neighbourhood that is central-ish to the University campus. So don't worry too much about the particular neighbourhood you end up in!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had no help from the University and the private housing market in Edinburgh is... a challenge. However, there are loads of opportunities to find a good place if you keep your eye out. And chances are you'll end up with some great people.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The online portal for course registration is arguably even more intuitive than the one UCPH uses. So you'll find no problem navigating it.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was no need for help, but the academic support seems well-equipped to handle any questions etc.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was eventually succesful. However, there was some initial confusion as to whether I could participate in postgraduate courses and be assessed for my work in them. Once that cleared up, I could choose the courses I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't worry too much about it.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Evaluating the level of the courses is difficult for a number of reasons. 1) You (or at least I did) spend more time studying, because you don't have a part-time job on the side. Overall, this means you're better prepared than you are in Denmark. At the same time, this is also expected from the lecturers, who expect more from you in terms of reflections before class. 2) The academic level is probably somewhat lower (if you visit at the end of your master's, like I did), but the exam format is quite different from what you're used to (essay-style short format). 3) Unless you're a native speaker, the language takes some time getting used to. Debating academic papers in English is just different than what I was used to (even though I had taken English courses in DK).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: In some cases, it was more engaging than what I have experienced in Denmark. Here, we could spend 20 minutes discussing a single paper or chapter of a book where everyone had a chance to contribute and reflect on the paper. I liked that.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1. Computational Text Analysis
2. International Political Economy
3. Comparative Analysis of Social and Public Policy

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
If you're into R, Natural Language Processing, sentiment analysis, machine learning etc., I would definitely recommend Computational Text Analysis. On the contrary, don't choose Comparative Analysis of Social and Public Policy - it does not cover anything you do not know from the
pol.sci
. bachelor's at KU.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The main unexpected cost was probably a 5500 DKK deposit for the room in the apartment.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Going out can be quite expensive if you're not solely frequenting student bars. Beers are probably 55 DKK and most venues take an entrance fee of approx 8-10 GBP.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not engage with them, but it seemed there were plenty of good opportunities.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All kinds.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Hiking is probably the biggest one. Go experience nature that we do not have in Denmark!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Travel to the country-side. The highlands are absolutely phenomenal, and the opportunities for traveling on a budget are quite good. It is a truly stunning country nature-wise. Also, see Glasgow - it's very different but also well worth a visit.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy as there's almost no language barrier and people are very friendly.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Not really, people are very welcoming and warm. You'll find no problem fitting in, I'm sure.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Half eight means 8.30 and not 7.30, like it would in Danish. Remember that.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Scots are more open and less reserved than Danes. That is a very charming trait and you'll find yourself striking up conversations with strangers all the time.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Enjoy it, because time flies past. 
2. Remember good shoes - you'll be walking around A LOT. 
3. Bring a rain jacket.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people. It is a massive gift to meet people that give new perspectives on things you assumed were universal truths.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Not spending too much money, I think. Remember to apply for as many scholarships as you can!

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Don't worry too much about all the planning. It'll take care of itself as you go along. Whether it's Edinburgh or somewhere else, just GO! We are in such a position of privilege to be able to bring SU and Erasmus grants to travel, so please capitalise on that.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
